content: 1. A study published in PLoS One in 2015 (Volume 10, Issue 12, Article e0144173) discusses the transmission of malaria and its implications for public health interventions. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) released guidelines in 2006 for testing mosquito adulticides used in indoor residual spraying (IRS) and the treatment of mosquito nets, emphasizing the importance of standardized evaluation methods. 3. In 2022, WHO published a document outlining the preferred product characteristics for indoor residual surface treatments aimed at controlling malaria transmission in areas with insecticide-resistant mosquito populations. 4. WHO's 2019 publication provides detailed data requirements and protocols for determining the non-inferiority of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) and IRS products within an established WHO policy class. 5. The second edition of the inter-agency field handbook on malaria control in humanitarian emergencies, published by WHO in 2013, offers comprehensive guidance for managing malaria outbreaks in crisis settings. 6. A 1993 study in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 87, Issue 6, Pages 620-626) highlights the effectiveness of bed nets in preventing malaria and anemia during pregnancy. 7. Research conducted by Moren A. in 1994 (Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, Volume 88, Issue 2, Pages 155-159) demonstrates the efficacy of permethrin-impregnated bed nets in reducing malaria incidence among schoolchildren on the Thai-Burmese border. 8. Rowland et al. (1996) investigated the use of pyrethroid-impregnated bed nets for personal protection against malaria among Afghan refugees, as published in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 90, Issue 4, Pages 357-361). 9. A 1997 study by Rowland et al. in the same journal (Volume 91, Issue 3, Pages 252-255) examined the transmission and control of vivax malaria in Afghan refugee settlements in Pakistan. 10. Rowland et al. (2000) conducted a community-randomized trial in Pakistan, demonstrating that indoor residual spraying with alpha-cypermethrin effectively controls malaria. This study was published in Tropical Medicine & International Health (Volume 5, Issue 7, Pages 472-481). 11. Smithuis et al. (2013) evaluated the impact of insecticide-treated bed nets on malaria incidence and prevalence among children in western Myanmar, an area with unstable seasonal transmission. The findings were published in Malaria Journal (Volume 12, Article 363). 12. Messenger et al. (2021) developed a protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis on vector control for malaria prevention during humanitarian emergencies, as published in BMJ Open (Volume 11, Issue 7, Article e046325). 13. Pryce, Richardson, and Lengeler (2018) reviewed the effectiveness of insecticide-treated nets for malaria prevention in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 11). 14. WHO convened a technical consultation in 2021 to determine the non-inferiority of vector control products within an established class, with the findings published in a report. 15. A pragmatic, cluster-randomized trial embedded in Uganda's national LLIN distribution campaign (LLINEUP) assessed the impact of long-lasting insecticidal nets with and without piperonyl butoxide on malaria indicators. The results were published in The Lancet (2020, Volume 395, Issue 10232, Pages 1292-1303). 16. Protopopoff et al. (2018) conducted a cluster-randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of long-lasting piperonyl butoxide-treated insecticidal nets and IRS interventions against pyrethroid-resistant mosquitoes. The study was published in The Lancet (Volume 391, Issue 10130, Pages 1577-1588). 17. Gleave et al. (2021) reviewed the use of piperonyl butoxide combined with pyrethroids in insecticide-treated nets for malaria prevention in Africa, as published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 5, Article CD012776). 18. Mosha et al. (2022) compared the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of three types of dual-active-ingredient LLINs with pyrethroid-only LLINs in Tanzania. The findings were published in The Lancet (Volume 399, Issue 10331, Pages 1227-1241). 19. Accrombessi et al. (2023) evaluated the efficacy of pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid and chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid LLINs compared to pyrethroid-only LLINs for malaria control in Benin. The study was published in The Lancet (Volume 401, Issue 10375, Pages 435-446). 20. Tiono et al. (2018) conducted a cluster-randomized controlled trial in Burkina Faso to compare the efficacy of Olyset Duo nets (containing pyriproxyfen and permethrin) with permethrin-only nets in areas with highly pyrethroid-resistant vectors. The results were published in The Lancet (Volume 392, Issue 10147, Pages 569-580). 21. WHO's 2017 publication emphasizes achieving and maintaining universal coverage with LLINs for malaria control. 22. WHO's 2014 recommendations address the sound management of old LLINs to ensure environmental safety and sustainability. 23. The second edition of WHO's operational manual on IRS for malaria transmission control and elimination was published in 2015. 24. The Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), updated in 2018, provides guidelines for managing chemicals that pose risks to human health and the environment. 25. WHO's 2017 meeting report discusses the comparative effectiveness of new vector control tools for malaria prevention. 26. WHO's 2006 publication outlines the use of IRS for scaling up global malaria control and elimination efforts. 27. The WHO Expert Committee on Malaria's sixth report, published in 1956, provides foundational insights into malaria control strategies. 28. Abuaku et al. (2018) investigated the impact of IRS on malaria parasitemia in northern Ghana, with findings published in Parasites & Vectors (Volume 11, Article 555). 29. Tseng et al. (2008) demonstrated the rapid control of malaria through IRS with alpha-cypermethrin in São Tomé and Príncipe, as published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 78, Issue 2, Pages 248-250). 30. Keating et al. (2021) retrospectively evaluated the effectiveness of IRS with pirimiphos-methyl (Actellic) on malaria transmission in Zambia, as published in Malaria Journal (Volume 20, Article 173). 31. Namuganga et al. (2021) examined the impact of stopping and restarting IRS on malaria burden in Uganda, with findings published in Nature Communications (Volume 12, Article 2635). 32. Gimnig et al. (2016) assessed the effect of IRS on malaria prevalence, clinical malaria, and anemia in western Kenya, as published in PLoS One (Volume 11, Issue 1, Article e0145282). 33. Curtis et al. (1998) compared the use of pyrethroids for house spraying versus bed net treatment against malaria vectors, as published in Tropical Medicine & International Health (Volume 3, Issue 8, Pages 619-631). 34. Misra et al. (1999) conducted a community-randomized trial in India to compare the effectiveness of bed nets and spraying with deltamethrin for malaria control, as published in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 93, Issue 5, Pages 456-457). 35. Abong'o et al. (2020) evaluated the impact of IRS with pirimiphos-methyl (Actellic 300CS) on entomological indicators and malaria case burden in western Kenya, as published in Scientific Reports (Volume 10, Article 4518). 36. Hailu et al. (2018) analyzed the cost-effectiveness of combining LLINs and IRS compared to each intervention alone for malaria prevention in Ethiopia, as published in Cost Effectiveness and Resource Allocation (Volume 16, Article 61). 37. Loha et al. (2019) reported that LLINs and IRS may not be sufficient to eliminate malaria in low-incidence areas, based on a cluster-randomized controlled trial in Ethiopia, as published in Malaria Journal (Volume 18, Article 141). 38. Longman et al. (2022) conducted a comparative cost analysis of PMI IRS country programs, published by the PMI VectorLink Project. 39. Gunasekaran et al. (2005) demonstrated that DDT IRS remains an effective tool for controlling Anopheles fluviatilis-transmitted Plasmodium falciparum malaria in India, as published in Tropical Medicine & International Health (Volume 10, Issue 2, Pages 160-168). 40. WHO's 2017 publication outlines data requirements and methods for evaluating new vector control products. 41. WHO's 2023 technical consultation assessed the comparative efficacy of vector control products, with findings published in a meeting report. 42. WHO's Malaria Policy Advisory Group (MPAG) meeting report from April 2023 provides updated recommendations for malaria control. 43. Bhatia et al. (2004) analyzed the cost-effectiveness of malaria control interventions in India, comparing ITNs and IRS, as published in Social Science & Medicine (Volume 59, Issue 3, Pages 525-539). 44. Pluess et al. (2010) reviewed the effectiveness of IRS for malaria prevention in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 4, Article CD006657). 45. A study in Acta Tropica (2001, Volume 80, Issue 1, Pages 1-8) evaluated the impact of IRS with malathion on malaria in refugee camps in eastern Sudan. 46. Mashauri et al. (2013) assessed the impact of IRS with lambda-cyhalothrin on malaria prevalence and anemia in northwestern Tanzania, as published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 88, Issue 5, Pages 841-849). 47. Guyatt et al. (2002) compared IRS and ITNs for malaria prevention in highland Kenya, as published in Tropical Medicine & International Health (Volume 7, Issue 4, Pages 298-303). 48. Rowland et al. (1997) investigated malaria prevalence in Afghan refugee villages sprayed with lambda-cyhalothrin or malathion, as published in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (Volume 88, Issue 4, Pages 378-379). 49. Wahid et al. (2016) conducted a cross-sectional study on heterogeneous malaria transmission in Afghan refugee populations in northern Pakistan, as published in Malaria Journal (Volume 15, Article 245). 50. Choi et al. (2019) reviewed the use of IRS for malaria prevention in communities using ITNs, as published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 5, Article CD012688). 51. WHO's 2014 guidance document provides recommendations for combining IRS and LLINs for malaria control. 52. WHO's 2015 information note highlights the risks associated with scaling back vector control after malaria transmission has been reduced. 53. Maia et al. (2018) reviewed the use of mosquito repellents for malaria prevention in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 2, Article CD011595). 54. Gabaldón Figuera et al. (2023) reviewed the effectiveness of topical repellents for malaria prevention, as published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 8, Article CD015422). 55. WHO's 2018 housing and health guidelines emphasize the role of housing improvements in vector control and sustainable development. 56. Tusting et al. (2017) analyzed the impact of housing improvements on malaria risk in sub-Saharan Africa, as published in PLoS Medicine (Volume 14, Issue 2, Article e1002234). 57. WHO's 2013 operational manual on larval source management provides guidance on this supplementary measure for malaria vector control. 58. Choi et al. (2019) reviewed the use of larviciding for malaria prevention in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 8, Article CD012736). 59. Walshe et al. (2017) reviewed the use of larvivorous fish for malaria prevention in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 12, Article CD008090). 60. Pryce et al. (2018) reviewed the use of insecticide space spraying for malaria prevention in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 11, Article CD012689). 61. Furnival-Adams et al. (2021) reviewed house modifications for malaria prevention in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Issue 1, Article CD013398). 62. Getawen et al. (2018) explored the impact of house screening interventions on malaria incidence in Ethiopia, as published in Acta Tropica (Volume 181, Pages 84-94). 63. Kirby et al. (2017) evaluated the effect of house screening interventions on malaria vector exposure and anemia in children, as published in PLoS Medicine.
